title: CSC 2770 Module 6: The OSI Model
source: Module 6 - OSI Model slides (Jacob Strickler, CSC 2770: Introduction to Systems and Networking; adapted from Mr. Eric Brown and Dr. Mike Rogers)

questions.q: Which organization created the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) model?
choices: Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE)
questions.explain: The ISO created the OSI. ISO is the organization; OSI is the model it created to help understand and standardize networking.

questions.q: What does the acronym OSI stand for?
questions.explain: OSI = Open Systems Interconnection. It is the model; the ISO is the organization that created it.

questions.q: Into how many layers does the OSI model divide networking architecture?
questions.explain: Seven layers: Application (7), Presentation (6), Session (5), Transport (4), Network (3), Data Link (2), Physical (1).

questions.q: Which list gives the OSI layers in order from Layer 7 down to Layer 1?
choices: Application, Presentation, Session, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Application, Session, Presentation, Transport, Network, Data Link, Physical
Application, Presentation, Session, Network, Transport, Data Link, Physical
Application, Presentation, Transport, Session, Network, Data Link, Physical
questions.explain: 7 Application, 6 Presentation, 5 Session, 4 Transport, 3 Network, 2 Data Link, 1 Physical.

questions.q: What layer number is the Session Layer?
questions.explain: Session is Layer 5, between Presentation (6) and Transport (4).

questions.q: Which OSI layer is Layer 1, at the very bottom of the model?
questions.explain: Layer 1 is the Physical Layer. Layer 2 is Data Link, and the Application Layer is Layer 7 at the top.

questions.q: The Application Layer is Layer 1 of the OSI model.
questions.explain: The Application Layer is Layer 7, the topmost layer. Layer 1 is the Physical Layer.

questions.q: The Application Layer handles communication between which two things?
choices: A router and the next router on the path
The network card and the physical cable
A sender's buffer and a receiver's buffer
questions.explain: Layer 7 covers communication between end-user applications (the programs you interact with) and the network, including a user interface and protocols.

questions.q: Which protocol is used to retrieve content such as HTML pages and images from web servers?
questions.explain: HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) retrieves web content to enable web browsing.

questions.q: Which protocol sends email from clients to mail servers, or between mail servers?
questions.explain: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) sends electronic mail from clients to mail servers or between mail servers.

questions.q: An administrator needs to log in to another machine and run commands on it, with all traffic encrypted. Which protocol fits?
questions.explain: SSH (Secure Shell) provides remote access and command over another machine, with traffic encrypted.

questions.q: Which of these are security-enhanced variants of HTTP or FTP that add encryption?
questions.explain: HTTPS, FTPS, and SFTP are the security-enhanced variants that add encryption. SMTP is the email protocol and UDP is a Transport Layer protocol.

questions.q: In the HTTP request line 'GET / HTTP/1.1', what does the '/' represent?
questions.explain: A request line is method, path, protocol version: GET is the method, / is the path, HTTP/1.1 is the protocol version. Headers follow on later lines.

questions.q: In the HTTP response line 'HTTP/1.1 200 OK', what is 'OK'?
questions.explain: A response line is protocol version, status code, status message: HTTP/1.1, then 200 (code), then OK (message).

questions.q: Which of these appear on the first line of an HTTP response, before the headers?
questions.explain: Responses start with version, status code, status message (e.g., HTTP/1.1 200 OK). Method and path belong to the first line of a request.

questions.q: Email (SMTP) or web pages (HTTP) could, in principle, just be sent as file transfers (FTP). Why do separate protocols exist anyway?
choices: Each is designed and optimized for its own specific context
Each one runs at a different layer of the OSI model
FTP can only send files from servers to clients
Each protocol works with only one transport protocol
questions.explain: Each protocol is optimized for its context: SMTP handles recipients and attachments, HTTP gives a browser-friendly format, and FTP is optimized for navigating, uploading, and downloading raw files. All three are Application Layer protocols.

questions.q: Which of the following are responsibilities of the Presentation Layer?
questions.explain: Presentation (Layer 6) is responsible for translation, compression, and encryption. Segmentation is Transport (4), path determination is Network (3), and authentication is Session (5).

questions.q: Converting text from ASCII to EBCDIC so an older IBM system can understand it is an example of which Presentation Layer responsibility?
questions.explain: Data translation ensures data sent by one system can be understood by the other, e.g., ASCII to EBCDIC for old IBM systems.

questions.q: Older IBM systems represent characters using which format, instead of ASCII or Unicode?
questions.explain: Older IBM systems use EBCDIC (Extended Binary Coded Decimal Interchange Code), a completely different format from ASCII/Unicode.

questions.q: One reason data translation is needed is that some systems use Little Endian byte order while others use Big Endian.
questions.explain: Systems differ in character encoding (ASCII/Unicode vs. EBCDIC) and in byte order (Little vs. Big Endian), so data must be translatable across systems.

questions.q: Most compression methods reduce the number of bits sent across a network by:
choices: Taking advantage of patterns in the data
Converting data into an unreadable format
Breaking data into small numbered segments
Switching to a different character encoding
questions.explain: Compression methods vary, but they tend to leverage patterns to express the same concept with less data. An unreadable format is encryption; segments belong to the Transport Layer.

questions.q: Using Run Length Encoding in the same style as the slides (count followed by character, like 5A 4B), encode the string XXXXYYYYYYYZZ.
questions.explain: Group the runs: XXXX (4), YYYYYYY (7), ZZ (2). Write each run as count + character: 4X 7Y 2Z.

questions.q: Decode the Run Length Encoded string 2M 3N 1P back into its original form.
questions.explain: 2M = MM, 3N = NNN, 1P = P, giving MMNNNP.

questions.q: Which kind of compression must be used for text files and executables?
choices: Lossless, so the original can be reconstructed perfectly
Lossy, because these files are mostly redundant data
Lossy, because smaller files transfer more efficiently
Either type, since small changes are harmless to them
questions.explain: Lossless compression (e.g., ZIP) lets the original be perfectly reconstructed, which is essential for text files, executables, etc.

questions.q: Which of these is an example of lossy compression?
questions.explain: JPEG is lossy: less important or redundant data is removed entirely. ZIP and RLE are lossless; EBCDIC is a character encoding, not compression.

questions.q: Run Length Encoding, as in the slide example (AAAAABBBBCCCCCCCDDDDEEE becomes 5A 4B 7C 4D 3E), is lossless.
questions.explain: The original string can be rebuilt exactly from the counts and characters, so nothing is lost.

questions.q: Data encryption (converting data into an unreadable format that the intended recipient can reverse) is listed as a responsibility of which layer?
questions.explain: Encryption, alongside translation and compression, is a Presentation Layer responsibility. Protocols like SSH and HTTPS that use encryption are Application Layer protocols, but the encryption function itself is listed under Layer 6.

questions.q: At the Session Layer, what is a 'session'?
choices: A single, continuous exchange of data between two devices
One packet routed from a host to its final destination
A group of hosts that share the same network portion
The set of protocols that a single application uses
questions.explain: The Session Layer (5) manages the session between two communicating devices: a single, continuous exchange of data.

questions.q: Which step of negotiating a session answers the question 'What are you allowed to do?'
questions.explain: Authorization checks permissions (what are you allowed to do?). Authentication verifies identity (who are you?).

questions.q: While a session is being set up, a server checks a username and password to verify who is connecting. Which step is this?
questions.explain: Verifying the identity of a user or device (who are you?) is authentication.

questions.q: What does full duplex communication allow?
choices: Both endpoints to communicate at the same time
Only one endpoint to communicate at a time
The receiver to set the sender's speed
Data to reach multiple hosts at once
questions.explain: Full duplex lets both endpoints communicate simultaneously, like a phone or video call. Half duplex allows only one at a time.

questions.q: Two devices agree that only one of them may send at a time, so they must take turns. What is this called?
questions.explain: Half duplex allows only one endpoint to communicate at a time; the endpoints take turns.

questions.q: At the Session Layer, the choice between full duplex and half duplex is determined by the physical medium (such as the type of cable).
questions.explain: This Layer 5 decision is based on protocol, not on the physical medium.

questions.q: Which of these may be involved in negotiating a session?
choices: Agreeing on who gets to talk, and when
questions.explain: Negotiating a session may involve authentication, authorization, and agreeing on the structure of the conversation. Segmentation is Transport (4); logical addressing is Network (3).

questions.q: Which of the following are responsibilities of the Transport Layer?
questions.explain: Transport (Layer 4) handles segmentation, flow control, and error control. Logical addressing is Network (3); compression is Presentation (6).

questions.q: Which Transport Layer responsibility adjusts the speed or quantity of transmissions based on the receiver's capacity?
questions.explain: Flow control makes sure the host sends data at a rate the destination can receive.

questions.q: Which Transport Layer responsibility ensures data is delivered correctly by detecting corruption and resending lost data (if desired)?
questions.explain: Error control ensures correct delivery: detecting corruption and resubmitting lost data if desired.

questions.q: A server can send at 100 Mbps, and a tablet can accept 25 Mbps. The server starts sending at 60 Mbps. What happens?
choices: Buffer overflow: data may be lost at the tablet
Buffer underflow: data may be lost at the tablet
Buffer underflow: no data loss, but slow performance
Buffer overflow: no data loss, but slow performance
questions.explain: Sending faster than the receiver can accept causes buffer overflow, and data may be lost at the receiving end. The receiver can tell the host to slow down.

questions.q: A server can send at 100 Mbps, and a tablet can accept 25 Mbps. The server sends at only 5 Mbps. What happens?
choices: Buffer overflow: data may be lost at the tablet
Buffer underflow: data may be lost at the tablet
Buffer underflow: no data loss, but slow performance
Buffer overflow: no data loss, but slow performance
questions.explain: Sending too slowly is buffer underflow: no data is lost, but performance is compromised. The receiver can tell the host to speed up.

questions.q: A server can send at 100 Mbps, and a tablet can accept at most 25 Mbps. Once flow control has adjusted the transmission, what rate (in Mbps) should the server be sending at?
questions.explain: The receiver tells the host how much it can accept, and the host adjusts to match: 25 Mbps. Faster causes overflow (data loss); slower causes underflow (wasted performance).

questions.q: How does flow control correct a host that is sending too fast or too slowly?
choices: The receiver tells the host how much data it can accept
The host asks a router to drop the extra packets
The two devices switch from full to half duplex
The host compresses data until the rates match
questions.explain: The receiver sends data back to the host explaining how much it can accept ('Slow down!' or 'Speed up!'), and the host adjusts its transmission speed.

questions.q: Which Transport Layer protocol provides reliable, well-ordered transmission with error checking?
questions.explain: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) is reliable, well-ordered, and error-checked. UDP is unreliable and unordered; IP is a Network Layer protocol; SMTP is an Application Layer protocol.

questions.q: Which of these typically use UDP rather than TCP?
questions.explain: UDP suits voice calls, online games, and streaming, where performance and real-time engagement matter more than reliability. Email, file transfers, and web browsing use TCP, where correctness matters more.

questions.q: Why is TCP the right choice for email?
choices: Getting an email slowly beats getting one with corrupted contents
TCP has lower latency than UDP for short text messages
UDP can only carry audio and video, not plain text
Mail servers accept connections only in half duplex
questions.explain: TCP favors correctness over performance: we would rather receive an email more slowly than receive one with its contents corrupted.

questions.q: Why does UDP have lower latency than TCP?
choices: It has less overhead and does not wait to recover or reorder packets
It compresses each segment before sending to reduce the bit count
It routes packets along shorter paths than TCP is allowed to use
It always uses full duplex, while TCP is limited to half duplex
questions.explain: UDP requires less overhead and doesn't wait to recover lost packets or reorder them, so there is less latency.

questions.q: UDP provides flow control but not error checking.
questions.explain: UDP provides neither: it is unreliable, unordered transmission without error checking or flow control.

questions.q: Which networking devices operate at the Network Layer (Layer 3)?
questions.explain: The Network Layer routes packets across networks to their destinations; it is the layer in which routers are involved.

questions.q: Which of these are elements of the Network Layer?
questions.explain: Network Layer elements are logical addressing (identifying devices across the network) and path determination/routing (finding the optimal course and moving packets along it).

questions.q: What is the most prominent Network Layer protocol, responsible for most logical addressing?
questions.explain: IP is the most prominent Network Layer protocol. TCP and UDP are Transport Layer protocols; HTTP is an Application Layer protocol.

questions.q: Every IP address is globally unique.
questions.explain: Each device on a network has a unique IP address used for routing, but IP addresses are not globally unique.

questions.q: How many bits make up an IPv4 address?
questions.explain: An IPv4 address is 32 bits, written as four 8-bit decimal values separated by dots (e.g., 192.168.5.12).

questions.q: How many unique IPv4 addresses are possible? (Give the exact number.)
questions.explain: 32 bits give 2^32 = 4,294,967,296 possible addresses, about 4.2 billion.

questions.q: Treating 192.168.5.12 as a traditional Class C address, which part is the host portion?
questions.explain: As a traditional Class C address, 192.168.5 is the network portion (which network the host is on) and 12 is the host portion (the individual device).

questions.q: The address 150.20.30.40 is split into 2 network octets and 2 host octets. What is the network portion?
questions.explain: The network portion is always at the beginning, so with 2 network octets it is 150.20; the host portion is 30.40.

questions.q: The network portion of an IPv4 address is always 3 octets, and the host portion is always 1 octet.
questions.explain: The split varies. 192.168.5.12 could be split 3/1, 2/2, or 1/3 depending on how many bits go to the network.

questions.q: In an IPv4 address, the network portion always comes at the beginning and the host portion always comes at the end.
questions.explain: The network portion is always first and the host portion always last, even though their sizes vary.

questions.q: In what year were IPv4 addresses introduced?
questions.explain: IPv4 addresses were introduced in 1981 and are the most commonly used IP addresses.

questions.q: Under classful networking, which class does 127.0.0.1 belong to?
questions.explain: Class A covers 0.0.0.0 to 127.255.255.255. A first octet of 127 is the top of the Class A range.

questions.q: Under classful networking, which class does 172.30.4.9 belong to?
questions.explain: Class B covers 128.0.0.0 to 191.255.255.255. A first octet of 172 falls in 128-191.

questions.q: Under classful networking, which class does 223.10.20.30 belong to?
questions.explain: Class C covers 192.0.0.0 to 223.255.255.255. A first octet of 223 is the top of the Class C range.

questions.q: Under classful networking, which class does 230.5.5.5 belong to?
questions.explain: Class D covers 224.0.0.0 to 239.255.255.255 and is used for multicast.

questions.q: Under classful networking, which class does 245.1.1.1 belong to?
questions.explain: Class E covers 240.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 and is reserved for experimental purposes.

questions.q: Using the classful address ranges, how can you tell which class an IPv4 address belongs to?
choices: Look at the value of the first octet
Look at the value of the last octet
Count how many octets are non-zero
questions.explain: The class ranges split on the first octet: 0-127 A, 128-191 B, 192-223 C, 224-239 D, 240-255 E.

questions.q: Which class allows a small number of networks, each with a large number of devices, and was intended for governments and very large organizations?
questions.explain: Class A: few networks, many devices each, for governments and very large organizations.

questions.q: Which class allows more networks than Class A but fewer devices per network, and was intended for medium-sized organizations and internet service providers (ISPs)?
questions.explain: Class B sits between A and C and was intended for medium-sized organizations and ISPs.

questions.q: Which class allows a large number of networks with a smaller number of devices each, and was intended for small businesses and personal home networks?
questions.explain: Class C: many networks, fewer devices each, for small businesses and home networks.

questions.q: What is Class D used for?
questions.explain: Class D is not used for standard networking; it is used for multicast communication. Experimental use is Class E.

questions.q: What does multicasting mean?
choices: Sending data to multiple, but not all, hosts at once
Sending data to every host on the network at once
Sending data to exactly one host at a time
Sending data only to the router for the network
questions.explain: Multicasting sends data to multiple (but not all) hosts at once, as in video calls and online games.

questions.q: Class E addresses are reserved for experimental purposes and are not used on the public Internet.
questions.explain: Class E is not used for standard networking; it is reserved for experimental, research and development purposes.

questions.q: Which of the following are problems with classful networking?
choices: Fixed size: every network in a class gets the same number of host addresses
Inefficiency: the address space assigned to each network is too large
Space exhaustion: addresses run out faster than they otherwise would
Unreliability: packets on Class C networks may arrive out of order
Insecurity: classful addresses expose traffic to eavesdroppers
questions.explain: The three problems are fixed size, inefficiency (e.g., Class A networks can have up to 16 million hosts each), and space exhaustion, which the first two cause.

questions.q: Under classful networking, a single Class A network can have up to roughly how many hosts?
questions.explain: Class A networks can have up to about 16 million hosts each, which is why classful assignment is inefficient. 4.2 billion is the size of the whole IPv4 space.

questions.q: About 4.2 billion IPv4 addresses is plenty to accommodate all network devices, so running out of addresses is not a concern.
questions.explain: 4.2 billion is not a large number for all network devices. Classful networking's fixed size and inefficiency make the space run out even faster.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: a web browser requests an HTML page using HTTP?
questions.explain: HTTP is an Application Layer protocol, used for web browsing.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: a photo is shrunk with JPEG compression before it is sent?
questions.explain: Compression (lossless or lossy, like JPEG) is a Presentation Layer responsibility.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: two devices verify each other's identity and agree on who gets to talk, and when?
questions.explain: Authentication and agreeing on the structure of the conversation are part of negotiating a session at Layer 5.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: a file is broken into segments that are reassembled at the destination?
questions.explain: Segmentation is a Transport Layer responsibility.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: a router determines the best path for a packet to reach another network?
questions.explain: Path determination/routing is a Network Layer element, and routers work at the Network Layer.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: a phone tells a server to slow down because data is being lost to buffer overflow?
questions.explain: Adjusting transmission speed to the receiver's capacity is flow control, a Transport Layer responsibility.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: text from an older IBM system is converted from EBCDIC so a modern system can read it?
questions.explain: Data translation between representations (ASCII/EBCDIC, Little/Big Endian) is a Presentation Layer responsibility.

questions.q: Which OSI layer handles this task: each device is given a logical address so it can be identified across the network?
questions.explain: Logical addressing (mostly handled by IP) is a Network Layer element.
